title: Planck's Law of Blackbody Radiation
short_intro: Planck's law describes the spectral radiance of electromagnetic radiation emitted from a blackbody in thermal equilibrium at a definite temperature T. It successfully resolves the ultraviolet catastrophe by postulating the quantization of energy in discrete packets known as photons or quanta.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of blackbody radiation, graphical variation of spectral emissive power with wavelength at different temperatures, Wien's displacement law, and Stefan-Boltzmann law as limiting cases.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of Planck's radiation formula using Bose-Einstein statistics or phase space density of states, derivation of Wien's law and Rayleigh-Jeans law from Planck's law, and calculation of total energy density.

concept_notes.heading: Blackbody Radiation and Spectral Energy Density
bullets: A blackbody is an idealized physical body that absorbs all incident electromagnetic radiation, regardless of frequency or angle of incidence.

The spectral energy density u(&#95lambda;, T) d&#95lambda; represents the amount of radiant energy per unit volume in the wavelength range between &#95lambda; and &#95lambda; + d&#95lambda; inside an isothermal cavity.
Classical physics (Rayleigh-Jeans law) predicted infinite energy at short wavelengths, an inconsistency known as the ultraviolet catastrophe.

concept_notes.heading: Quantum Hypothesis of Max Planck
bullets: Planck assumed that the oscillators comprising the blackbody walls can only emit or absorb energy in discrete packets or quanta of magnitude E = hν.
Here, h is Planck's constant (6.626 × 10<sup>-34</sup> J⋅s) and ν is the frequency of the oscillator.
This revolutionary postulate abandoned the classical continuous energy distribution and laid the foundation of quantum mechanics.

concept_notes.heading: Derivation Framework and Density of Modes
bullets: The derivation combines the number of standing electromagnetic wave modes per unit volume in a cavity with the average energy of a quantum oscillator.
The number of standing wave modes per unit volume for frequency interval &#95nu; to &#95nu; + d&#95nu; is given by 8π&#95nu;<sup>2</sup>d&#95nu;/c<sup>3</sup>.
Using Maxwell-Boltzmann or Bose-Einstein statistics, the average energy of an oscillator at temperature T is given by h&#95nu; / (exp(h&#95nu;/k_B T) - 1).

concept_notes.heading: Limiting Cases of Planck's Law
bullets: At very long wavelengths (low frequencies), h&#95nu; << k_B T, Planck's law reduces to the classical Rayleigh-Jeans law: u(&#95lambda;)d&#95lambda; = (8πk_B T / &#95lambda;<sup>4</sup>)d&#95lambda;.
At short wavelengths (high frequencies), Planck's law reduces to Wien's radiation law.
Integrating Planck's law over all wavelengths yields the Stefan-Boltzmann law, where total emissive power is proportional to T<sup>4</sup>.

derivations.title: Derivation of Wien's Displacement Law from Planck's Law
derivations.conditions: Finding the wavelength corresponding to maximum spectral radiance
steps: Express Planck's law in terms of wavelength &#95lambda; by substituting &#95nu; = c/&#95lambda;: u(\lambda, T)d\lambda = \frac{8\pi h c}{\lambda^5} \frac{1}{\exp(\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}) - 1} d\lambda.
Differentiate the spectral energy density with respect to &#95lambda; and set the derivative equal to zero: \frac{du(\lambda, T)}{d\lambda} = 0.
Let x = \frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}. The differentiation condition simplifies to the transcendental equation (5 - x)e^x = 5.
Solve numerically for x ≈ 4.965, yielding \lambda_{max} T = \frac{hc}{4.965 k_B T} \times T = \text{constant}.

formula_sheet.name: Planck's Law (Frequency Form)
formula_sheet.variables: u(&#95nu;, T) = spectral energy density, h = Planck's constant, &#95nu; = frequency, c = speed of light, k_B = Boltzmann constant, T = absolute temperature
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for all frequencies at thermal equilibrium

formula_sheet.name: Planck's Law (Wavelength Form)
formula_sheet.equation_html: u(\lambda, T)d\lambda = \frac{8\pi h c}{\lambda^5} \frac{1}{\exp(\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}) - 1} d\lambda
formula_sheet.variables: u(&#95lambda;, T) = spectral energy density per unit wavelength, &#95lambda; = wavelength
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for all wavelengths at thermal equilibrium

formula_sheet.name: Rayleigh-Jeans Law
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid only for very long wavelengths (h&#95nu; << k_B T)

formula_sheet.name: Wien's Radiation Law
formula_sheet.equation_html: u_W(\lambda, T)d\lambda = \frac{8\pi h c}{\lambda^5} \exp\left(-\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}\right) d\lambda
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid only for very short wavelengths (h&#95nu; >> k_B T)

formula_sheet.name: Wien's Displacement Law
formula_sheet.variables: &#95lambda;<sub>max</sub> = wavelength of maximum emission, b = Wien's constant (2.898 × 10<sup>-3</sup> m⋅K)
formula_sheet.conditions: Applies to the peak of the blackbody spectrum

formula_sheet.name: Stefan-Boltzmann Law
formula_sheet.variables: E = total emissive power, &#96sigma; = Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67 × 10<sup>-8</sup> W/m<sup>2</sup>K<sup>4</sup>)
formula_sheet.conditions: Integrated over all wavelengths for a perfect blackbody

formula_sheet.name: Average Energy of Planck Oscillator
formula_sheet.variables: ⟨E⟩ = mean thermal energy of oscillator of frequency &#95nu;

formula_sheet.name: Planck's Emissive Power Form (Spectral Radiance)
formula_sheet.equation_html: E_{\lambda}(\lambda, T) = \frac{c}{4} u(\lambda, T) = \frac{2\pi h c^2}{\lambda^5} \frac{1}{\exp(\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}) - 1}
formula_sheet.variables: E_&#95lambda; = spectral emissive power per unit area per unit wavelength

graphs_and_experiments.title: Blackbody Spectral Radiance vs Wavelength
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of spectral energy density (or emissive power) on the y-axis against wavelength on the x-axis for multiple increasing temperatures T_1, T_2, T_3. Show peaks shifting to shorter wavelengths as temperature increases without curves intersecting.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Each curve has a distinct maximum at &#95lambda;<sub>max</sub>. The area under each curve represents total energy emitted (proportional to T<sup>4</sup>). As temperature rises, peak shifts to left (shorter wavelength) and height increases dramatically.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Extensively tested in TGT and PGT for qualitative shifts, validating Wien's displacement law, and comparing with classical Rayleigh-Jeans failure at small wavelengths.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Comparison of Planck's Law with Classical Approximations
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A single logarithmic or linear plot showing Planck's curve matching experimental data completely, with the Rayleigh-Jeans curve diverging at ultraviolet wavelengths and Wien's curve diverging at infrared wavelengths.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Highlights the ultraviolet catastrophe predicted by classical equipartition theorem and demonstrates how Planck's interpolation formula bridges long and short wavelength regimes perfectly.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual PGT questions regarding the limits where classical laws fail or hold true.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fery's Blackbody Cavity Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A hollow sphere with a small conical projection inside, a tiny aperture for radiation entry/exit, and double-walled construction for thermal insulation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Any radiation entering through the aperture undergoes multiple internal reflections, with total absorption probability approaching unity, creating an experimental realization of a blackbody.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct factual questions in TGT/PGT regarding the construction and working principle of artificial blackbodies.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the wavelength of maximum emission for a star emitting radiation like a blackbody at a temperature of 5800 K. Take Wien's constant b = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.
solution_steps: Identify given values: T = 5800 K, b = 2.898 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m\cdot K}.

solved_numericals.question: Using Planck's radiation law, find the ratio of spectral energy densities at wavelength &#95lambda; = 500 nm for a blackbody at temperatures T_1 = 3000 K and T_2 = 6000 K in the Wien approximation limit.
solution_steps: Check validity of Wien's approximation: For &#95lambda; = 500 nm and T = 3000 K, \frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^8)}{(500 \times 10^{-9})(1.38 \times 10^{-23})(3000)} \approx 9.58 >> 1, so Wien's law is valid.

Write Wien's approximation ratio: \frac{u(\lambda, T_2)}{u(\lambda, T_1)} = \frac{\lambda^{-5} \exp(-hc / \lambda k_B T_2)}{\lambda^{-5} \exp(-hc / \lambda k_B T_1)} = \exp\left[ \frac{hc}{\lambda k_B} \left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right) \right].

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature will the total energy density of radiation inside a blackbody cavity be 1.0 J/m^3? (Stefan-Boltzmann constant &#96sigma; = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2K^4, speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s). Note: Energy density u = (4/c) \sigma T^4.
solution_steps: Rearrange the relation for temperature: T^4 = \frac{u \cdot c}{4 \sigma}.
Substitute given values: u = 1.0 \text{ J/m}^3, c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}, \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \text{ W/m}^2\text{K}^4.
Take the fourth root: T = (1.3228 \times 10^{15})^{1/4} \approx 1899 \text{ K}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The cavity walls are made of material that contains harmonic oscillators of all frequencies in thermal equilibrium.
Limitation: Planck's law assumes isotropic and unpolarized radiation inside an ideal vacuum cavity; real surfaces have emissivities less than unity (gray bodies).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Planck's law applies only to visible light emitted by hot objects.
common_misconceptions.correct: Planck's law applies to electromagnetic radiation across the entire continuous spectrum, including ultraviolet, visible, infrared, and microwave regions.
common_misconceptions.why: A blackbody emits radiation over all wavelengths simultaneously, with the distribution determined entirely by temperature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The ultraviolet catastrophe was resolved by introducing higher order wave corrections in classical electrodynamics.
common_misconceptions.correct: The ultraviolet catastrophe was resolved by discarding classical continuous energy distribution and introducing discrete energy quanta (h&#95nu;).
common_misconceptions.why: Classical statistical mechanics (equipartition theorem) inherently fails at high frequencies because it assigns equal kT energy to all modes regardless of frequency.

quick_revision: Planck's law gives spectral energy density as u(&#95nu;) = (8πh&#95nu;<sup>3</sup> / c<sup>3</sup>) [1 / (exp(h&#95nu;/k_B T) - 1)].
At long wavelengths, Planck's law reduces to the Rayleigh-Jeans law.
Wien's displacement law states that &#95lambda;<sub>max</sub> T = constant.
Energy quantization (E = h&#95nu;) successfully eliminated the ultraviolet catastrophe.
